system.name: Litestream
system.purpose: A disaster-recovery sidecar for SQLite: it replicates a database to object storage continuously, without ever writing the database file itself.

sources.ref: db.go, replica.go, store.go, compactor.go, server.go, vfs.go, cmd/litestream/

sources.note: the SQLite API claim and the _litestream_lock behaviour

boundaries.label: Owned by SQLite
boundaries.claim: Litestream reaches all of this only through the SQLite API, which is why replicating cannot corrupt it

evidence.label: only communicates through the SQLite API

boundaries.label: The Litestream process
boundaries.claim: A sidecar: stop all of it and SQLite keeps serving reads and writes

components.name: litestream CLI
components.responsibility: Parses the command and either starts the long-running replication process or performs a one-shot restore.

components.name: Control socket
components.responsibility: Lets a running process be changed without restarting it, over a Unix socket.

components.name: Store
components.responsibility: Holds every registered database and schedules background work so the host is not overloaded by concurrent compactions.

components.name: DB
components.responsibility: Manages one SQLite database: watches the log, decides when to checkpoint, and turns committed pages into transaction files.

components.name: Replica
components.responsibility: Syncs one database's transaction files to one destination and tracks how far the destination has caught up.

components.name: Compactor
components.responsibility: Merges transaction files into higher levels and deletes what the retention policy no longer needs.

components.name: Leaser
components.responsibility: Holds and renews a lease so two processes never replicate to the same destination at once.

components.name: Replica client
components.responsibility: Speaks whichever destination protocol was configured, behind one interface the rest of the system uses.

components.name: Destination
components.responsibility: Stores transaction files and snapshots as plain objects.

components.name: SQLite database
components.responsibility: Holds the data your application reads and writes.

components.name: Write-ahead log
components.responsibility: Records the pages SQLite has committed, and is the only place Litestream learns what changed.

components.name: _litestream_lock
components.responsibility: Gives Litestream somewhere to take SQLite's write lock while it coordinates around a checkpoint.

components.name: Read-replica VFS
components.responsibility: Serves reads straight from the destination with no local copy of the database.
notes: Behind a build tag, so it is in the tree but not in a default build.

facts.claim: Litestream never writes your database or its log
facts.because: it reaches both only through SQLite's own API, so an interrupted replication cannot leave either in a state SQLite did not create

facts.claim: Replication is never in the path of a write
facts.because: a write returns as soon as SQLite commits, so a slow or unreachable destination costs recovery, never availability

facts.claim: Replicating adds a table to your database
facts.because: the write lock has to be held somewhere while a checkpoint is coordinated, and a restored copy therefore contains that table too
a lease stops two processes interleaving transaction files into the same place

facts.claim: Files are compacted into levels, never rewritten in place
facts.because: a restore replays a snapshot plus a contiguous range, so merging can shrink the history without being able to lose a transaction

facts.claim: Losing the destination costs recovery, not uptime
facts.because: the database keeps serving; what is gone is the ability to rebuild it elsewhere

questions.title: How a change reaches the destination
questions.ask: What happens between a committed transaction and an object in storage?
questions.answer: Litestream reads the pages SQLite already committed, packs them into transaction files, and a replica pushes them on an interval. The commit never waits for any of it.
questions.omits: Restore, compaction, and the control socket. Each is its own question.

questions.title: Why replicating cannot corrupt the database
questions.ask: A background process is touching a live database. Why is that safe?
questions.answer: Because it is not touching it. Every read and every checkpoint goes through SQLite's own API, and the write lock is taken in a table inside the database using a transaction that is always rolled back.
questions.omits: Everything past the replica; nothing downstream can reach back into the database.

questions.title: How a database is rebuilt
questions.ask: The machine is gone. What does it take to get the database back?
questions.answer: A snapshot and the contiguous transaction files recorded after it, replayed into a new file. Nothing from the lost machine is required, and the rebuilt copy carries the lock table with it.
questions.omits: The live replication path, which is not running during a restore.

questions.title: Keeping it running and keeping it small
questions.ask: What stops the history growing forever, or two processes fighting over one bucket?
questions.answer: A compactor merges transaction files into higher levels and expires what retention drops. A lease means only one process writes to a destination at a time.
questions.omits: How a transaction file is produced in the first place.
